An ultracrepidarian is a person who confidently gives opinions, judgments, or advice on subjects they know nothing — or very little — about.

The key idea is this: their confidence is wildly out of proportion to their actual knowledge. They don't just have wrong opinions. They voice those opinions as if they were an expert, on topics that are clearly beyond their understanding.

Think of it in two parts:

  • Lack of knowledge on a subject
  • Speaking anyway, with confidence and authority

Both parts must be present. A person who is ignorant but stays quiet is not an ultracrepidarian. A person who speaks confidently but actually does know their subject is definitely not one either. It is specifically the combination of not knowing + speaking as though you do that defines this word.

Example 1 — The dinner-table doctor
Your uncle has no medical training whatsoever. He has never studied medicine, biology, or pharmacology. But the moment someone at dinner mentions a health issue, he jumps in and confidently declares what disease it is, what the cause is, and what treatment should be followed. He doesn't say "I'm not sure, but..." — he states it as fact. That uncle is an ultracrepidarian.

Example 2 — The football fan coaching the coach
A person who has only ever watched football on television starts loudly explaining to a professional football coach what tactics are wrong and what the coach should do differently. He has never played the game competitively, never studied the sport strategically — but he speaks like a seasoned professional. That fan is being an ultracrepidarian.

Example 3 — The software critic
A person who has never written a single line of code in their life sits next to a senior software engineer and confidently tells her why her code is inefficient and how she should rewrite it. He doesn't frame it as a question. He frames it as obvious truth. He is an ultracrepidarian.

The common thread: they are operating far outside their lane, but they don't know it — or don't care.

• It is not simply being wrong. Everyone is wrong sometimes, even experts. An ultracrepidarian is specifically someone who is unqualified to be speaking in the first place.
  • It is not asking questions out of curiosity. Asking "Why do doctors do X?" is fine — that's learning. Declaring "Doctors should do X, they're clearly wrong" when you have no medical knowledge — that's the problem.
  • It is not just being ignorant. Ignorance alone is neutral. Many people don't know about many things, and that's normal. The ultracrepidarian is the one who turns that ignorance into loud, confident proclamation.

An ultracrepidarian typically has no awareness that they are out of their depth. This is what makes the word particularly cutting. They don't think "I don't really know this subject, but let me offer a tentative thought." They think "I have an opinion, therefore my opinion is valid and worth asserting."

This connects closely to a famous idea in psychology called the Dunning-Kruger effect — the tendency for people with limited knowledge in an area to overestimate their own competence in that area. An ultracrepidarian is essentially a real-world, walking example of this effect. Because they don't know enough about the subject to understand how much they don't know, they feel no reason to hold back.

Calling someone an ultracrepidarian is not neutral — it is a criticism, and quite a sharp one. It is a formal, intellectual-sounding word, which means it is typically used in serious writing, formal debate, or educated conversation. When someone uses it, they are usually making a pointed remark about someone else's arrogance or lack of self-awareness.

It is also a somewhat rare word, which means using it correctly in conversation or writing immediately signals that you have a refined vocabulary. It is the kind of word that makes people pause and look it up.
How to use it in a sentence

• "Don't take his advice on investing — he's never managed money in his life. He's a complete ultracrepidarian."
  • "The comment section was full of ultracrepidarians confidently diagnosing the patient based on a two-line news article."
  • "She grew tired of the ultracrepidarians at the meeting who had no engineering background but spoke as though they had designed bridges their whole careers."
One final image to lock it in

Imagine a person standing outside a hospital in a white coat they found somewhere, stopping patients and giving them diagnoses and prescriptions — with complete confidence — despite having zero medical training. Everyone around them can see they have no idea what they're doing. But they cannot see it themselves.

That image — unearned confidence, misplaced authority, blissful unawareness of one's own incompetence — is the soul of the word ultracrepidarian.
